item.title: One Disk for Everything Is One Bad Day Away
item.description: Separate your system and data onto two physical drives to prevent a single hardware failure from destroying your server and photos simultaneously.
item.content:encoded:
Most new homelabbers size their first server by the apps they want to run today. That is the trap. A single SSD holding Proxmox, every container, and your entire photo library looks simple on day one, and nothing about it looks wrong until that drive wears out or fills up. Then you lose the server and the data at the same moment, and the restore needs the very disk that died.

The book Self-Host Your Life opens its hardware chapter with exactly this warning under a heading that sums it up: the trap: one disk, one container, one bad day. This post covers the layout rule, how to separate system from data, and the exact VM configuration that keeps your photos safe when the OS disk fails.

One caveat, straight from the book: this guidance assumes you are building a foundation with Proxmox on a used business mini PC or similar hardware. If you already run services in LXC containers, the advice differs slightly, but the core principle of separating system and data remains critical for anyone starting out.

The rule: two physical drives, not one partition

The most common beginner layout is a single SSD holding Proxmox, the containers, and every photo you own. It works until that SSD wears out or the filesystem fills up. Then you lose the server and the data at the same moment. The fix is to use two physical drives with distinct roles:

  • Drive 1, a small SSD (256 to 512 GB): Proxmox itself and the virtual disks of your guests. Databases live here because they need fast, local storage.
  • Drive 2, a large HDD or SSD: your photo library, Nextcloud files, and backups that are waiting to go elsewhere. This is the drive that grows.

The second trap is subtler but equally dangerous. Immich’s own documentation says it runs well in a full virtual machine and that Docker inside an LXC container is not recommended, possible only for advanced users. While some run Immich in an LXC and it works, others spend evenings untangling permissions problems that a VM would never have had. If this is your first build, follow the recommendation to use a VM.

One VM with Docker is easier to back up, update, and reason about than three hand-built containers, and it is exactly what the Immich and Nextcloud projects test against. The recommended VM size requires at least 4 vCPUs and 8 GB of RAM, though 12 to 16 GB is comfortable if you run multiple apps.

The trap: ignoring CPU instruction sets

Immich alone asks for 6 GB of RAM minimum and 8 GB recommended, but the hardware requirement that catches people out is the CPU. Its machine-learning container needs a CPU with the x86-64-v2 instruction level. Anything from about 2012 onward has it, but in Proxmox you must set the VM’s CPU type to host or x86-64-v2-AES. The default on recent Proxmox installations is often correct, but if you select an older generic model, the container will fail to start.

This setting matters because modern consumer CPUs include features required for efficient image processing. If you do not set the CPU type correctly, you may spend time debugging why Immich refuses to launch, when the issue is simply a mismatch between the virtual hardware definition and the physical chip’s capabilities.

The fix: create the VM from the shell

To implement the two-drive strategy, you must create a Debian 13 virtual machine that explicitly attaches both drives. Download the Debian 13 netinst ISO to your Proxmox ISO storage, then create the VM from the Proxmox shell. Adjust storage names to your own configuration; for example, use local-lvm for the SSD and tank for the big drive.

The command below sets up a VM named docker01 with 12 GB of RAM, 4 cores, and the correct CPU type. It attaches the system disk to the SSD storage and the data disk to the large drive storage. The --onboot 1 flag ensures the VM starts automatically if Proxmox reboots.

qm create 201 --name docker01 --memory 12288 --cores 4 \
  --cpu host --machine q35 --bios ovmf \
  --efidisk0 local-lvm:1,efitype=4m \
  --scsihw virtio-scsi-single \
  --scsi0 local-lvm:100,ssd=1,discard=on,iothread=1 \
  --scsi1 tank:1000,iothread=1 \
  --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 --agent enabled=1 \
  --ide2 local:iso/debian-13-amd64-netinst.iso,media=cdrom \
  --boot order='scsi0;ide2' --onboot 1
qm start 201

Install Debian with no desktop environment and only "SSH server" and "standard system utilities" ticked. After the first boot, install the guest agent and Docker from Docker’s own repository. The distro’s docker.io package is older, and Immich’s documentation warns against it.

apt update && apt install -y qemu-guest-agent curl
systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sh get-docker.sh
docker compose version

Read get-docker.sh before you run it; it is a short script, and it is good practice never to pipe an unread script into a root shell. If you prefer, Docker’s documentation lists the manual apt repository steps for Debian.

The trap: relying on drive order instead of labels

Inside the VM, the second disk shows up as /dev/sdb. Formatting it once and mounting it by its label ensures that a reordered disk never mounts in the wrong place. If you mount by device name alone, a reboot might swap the identifiers, causing your system to boot without data or mount the OS drive into your photo folder.

The nofail option matters significantly here. If the data disk ever goes missing, the VM still boots and you can fix it over SSH instead of from a rescue console. Without nofail, a missing data disk could prevent the entire system from booting, leaving you locked out until you physically access the machine.

Format the data disk once and mount it by its label using these commands:

mkfs.ext4 -L data /dev/sdb
mkdir -p /srv/data
echo "LABEL=data /srv/data ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a && df -h /srv/data
mkdir -p /srv/data/{immich,nextcloud,backups}

If you insist on LXC containers instead of a VM, set two features on the container and keep it unprivileged. However, put the database on container-local storage, not on a bind-mounted share, and expect to solve the odd permissions puzzle. It is a perfectly good setup once it is stable, but it is a poor place to learn.

pct set 143 --features nesting=1,keyctl=1
pct reboot 143

Checklist: foundation

☐ System and guest disks on an SSD; photos and files on a separate data drive ☐ One Debian 13 VM as the Docker host, CPU type host or x86-64-v2-AES ☐ At least 8 GB of RAM for the VM (12 GB or more if you run all three apps) ☐ Docker installed from Docker's repository; docker compose version works ☐ Data disk mounted by label with nofail, and df -h shows it ☐ The VM starts at boot (--onboot 1) and the guest agent is running

item.title: Your Android App Has Native Code Even If You Never Wrote C++
item.description: Hidden .so files in ML and media libraries can block your app from Google Play. Learn to check alignment, fix build configs, and ensure 16 KB page support before the February 2027 deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Most developers assume their app has no native code because they never wrote a single line of C or C++. That assumption is the trap. Machine learning runtimes, video and audio libraries, database engines, image codecs, and some analytics SDKs all ship .so files. If one of these dependencies was built for 4 KB pages only, your app is not compliant with Google Play requirements, even if you did not write the native code yourself.

The requirement is strict: starting February 1, 2027, if your app updates do not support 16 KB memory page sizes, you will not be able to release them. For pure Kotlin or Java apps, this is not an issue. However, for any app with native code hidden inside a library, it can become a hard block on releasing updates. The following sections explain how to identify these hidden dependencies, verify their alignment, and apply the necessary fixes to your build configuration.

The Trap: Hidden Native Dependencies

The core misconception is that you are responsible only for the code you write. In reality, modern Android development relies heavily on third-party libraries that include precompiled native binaries. These .so files often go unnoticed during initial setup because they are bundled automatically with the app.

Google Play now requires all apps targeting Android 15 (API level 35) and higher to support 16 KB memory page sizes on 64-bit devices. While pure Kotlin and Java applications already support these devices, any native code must be aligned correctly. A shared library loaded into memory in segments must have each segment start on a 16 KB boundary. If a library is linked for 4 KB pages, its segments start on 4 KB boundaries, which can cause the library to fail to load or crash on newer devices.

The warning often appears in Play Console on someone else's code, not yours. This means you must audit your entire dependency tree, not just your source files. The deadline is fixed: February 1, 2027. After this date, non-compliant updates cannot be released to users.

Step 1: Identify and Verify Native Code Alignment

Before attempting any fixes, you must determine if your app contains native code and whether it is properly aligned. Android Studio provides a quick way to check this. Open Build > Analyze APK and select your release APK. Look in the lib folder. If it is missing or empty, the app has no native code, and you are done. If there are .so files, the Alignment column shows a warning for each file with an alignment problem. Android Studio and lint also flag prebuilt libraries that are not 16 KB aligned.

For a more rigorous verification, especially in a CI environment, you should check every library from the command line. You can unpack the APK and inspect the LOAD segments using tools from the SDK. Any LOAD line with align 213, 212, or lower indicates a library that needs rebuilding or replacing. The zipalign check ensures the package itself is stored correctly, ending with "Verification successful" when every library is aligned properly.

The following commands demonstrate how to perform these checks:

# 1. Unpack the APK
unzip -q app-release.apk -d /tmp/apk_out

# 2. Each LOAD segment must show align 2**14 (16 KB) or more
NDK_BIN="$ANDROID_NDK_HOME/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/linux-x86_64/bin"
for so in /tmp/apk_out/lib/arm64-v8a/*.so /tmp/apk_out/lib/x86_64/*.so; do
  [ -f "$so" ] || continue
  echo "$so"
  "$NDK_BIN/llvm-objdump" -p "$so" | grep LOAD
done

# 3. Zip alignment of the APK itself (Build-Tools 35.0.0 or newer)
"$ANDROID_HOME"/build-tools/35.0.0/zipalign -v -c -P 16 4 app-release.apk

For App Bundles, use bundletool to check the configuration:

bundletool dump config --bundle=app-release.aab | grep alignment

PAGE_ALIGNMENT_16K means the bundle asks for 16 KB zip alignment, while PAGE_ALIGNMENT_4K indicates that APKs built from it will have 4 KB aligned .so files.

Step 2: Fix the Build Configuration

The guide offers a straightforward path to compliance if you update your build tools. With AGP 8.5.1 or higher, NDK r28 or higher, and 16 KB compatible prebuilt dependencies, your app is 16 KB compatible by default. You must keep AGP current and ensure uncompressed packaging is used, as 16 KB devices require uncompressed shared libraries on a 16 KB zip-aligned boundary.

For your own C and C++ code, NDK r28 and later compile 16 KB aligned by default. You should pin the version in Gradle so every machine uses the same one:

android {
    // NDK r28+ produces 16 KB aligned libraries by default
    ndkVersion = "28.2.13676358"
}

If you are stuck on NDK r27 or older, you must add specific linker flags. With CMake, use:

target_link_options(${CMAKE_PROJECT_NAME} PRIVATE
    "-Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384"
    "-Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384")

With ndk-build, add this to Android.mk:

LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384

For prebuilt libraries from third parties, you cannot relink a binary you do not build. You must update the dependency to a version whose release notes say it supports 16 KB pages, or replace it entirely. The guide states that prebuilt shared libraries must be recompiled the same way and re-imported.

If you cannot upgrade AGP to 8.5.1 or higher, the guide suggests having Gradle compress the shared libraries by setting useLegacyPackaging = true. However, this is only a workaround for packaging; it does not fix a library whose ELF segments are 4 KB aligned. Furthermore, compression causes the app to take more space once installed.

Step 3: Update Code and Test

Even with aligned libraries, native code that hard-codes the page size can still break. You must remove any code that relies on the PAGE_SIZE constant or assumes pages are 4096 bytes. Instead, use getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE). Review mmap() calls and other APIs that need page-aligned arguments. Check custom memory allocators if you have any.

Finally, test the app on a 16 KB environment. Use an Android Emulator system image with 16 KB page size. Confirm the environment first:

adb shell getconf PAGE_SIZE      # should print 16384

Then exercise every feature that touches native code, such as ML models, video exports, and database operations. A library that loaded fine on 4 KB pages but crashes here is exactly what this step is designed to catch. Run these checks on every release build and fail the job if any LOAD segment is below 2**14.

Checklist

  • You know whether the release APK contains any .so files, including from libraries
  • AGP 8.5.1 or newer (AGP 9.4.0 at the time of writing) and NDK r28 or newer, pinned with ndkVersion
  • Every arm64-v8a and x86_64 library shows LOAD alignment 2**14 or higher
  • zipalign -c -P 16 reports "Verification successful"
  • No native code assumes a 4096-byte page
  • The app tested on a 16 KB emulator image (getconf PAGE_SIZE = 16384)
  • Done before February 1, 2027, when non-compliant updates can no longer be released

item.title: Trap: Using Debug Builds for Performance Benchmarks
item.description: You might measure performance using debug builds, but these contain overhead that skews results. Learn why you must use profileable release builds and the exact Gradle configuration to get accurate data.
item.content:encoded:
Most developers pick the tool they know first rather than the question they need answered. This leads to a specific, expensive trap: measuring performance using debug builds. Debug builds contain instrumentation and overhead that distort timing data. When you run benchmarks on these builds, you are not measuring how your app performs for users; you are measuring how fast it runs with extra diagnostic baggage attached. The result is misleading data that looks good in testing but fails in production.

The chapter "The Tools" in the book Fast by Default provides a map of which tool answers which question. It explicitly states that modern Android Studio versions can profile either a debuggable build with complete data or a profileable release build with low overhead. The rule is strict: use the low-overhead mode for anything about time; use complete data only when you need detail a profileable build cannot give, such as a heap dump with full allocation tracking. If you are measuring startup time, frame durations, or scrolling performance, you must use a release-like build that includes the `` tag.

The trap: benchmarking debug builds

The easiest way to start a benchmark is to run a test against your current build configuration. However, if you do not explicitly configure a separate benchmark build type, Android Studio may default to running tests against a debuggable variant. Debug builds include extensive logging and instrumentation that slow down execution. This overhead masks the true performance characteristics of your code. You might see acceptable frame times in development but encounter jank in production because the release build lacks the safety nets and includes optimizations that change timing behavior.

The book warns that Layout Inspector shows recomposition counts for debuggable builds, so it is a diagnostic tool, not a measuring tool. You should use it to find what recomposes, then confirm the effect on frame times with Macrobenchmark on a release build. This distinction applies to all timing measurements. If you want to know how long startup takes or if scrolling drops frames, you must use Macrobenchmark against a release-like build.

The fix: configure the benchmark module correctly

To avoid this trap, you need to set up a separate com.android.test module that targets your app module. This module handles the installation, control, and execution of benchmarks against a real release-like build. The book provides the exact Gradle configuration required for this setup. You must define the plugin IDs, namespace, and dependencies in your macrobenchmark module's build.gradle.kts file.

// macrobenchmark/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.test")
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android")
}
android {
    namespace = "com.example.fieldnotes.macrobenchmark"
    compileSdk = 36

    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 28
        testInstrumentationRunner = "androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner"
    }
    targetProjectPath = ":app"
    experimentalProperties["android.experimental.self-instrumenting"] = true
    buildTypes {
        create("benchmark") {
            isDebuggable = true
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
            matchingFallbacks += listOf("release")
        }
    }
}
dependencies {
    implementation("androidx.test.ext:junit:1.3.0")
    implementation("androidx.benchmark:benchmark-macro-junit4:1.5.0")
}

Notice that the benchmark module is debuggable, not the app. This allows the test runner to instrument the benchmark code while keeping the target app close to a real release state. The book also notes that you should take whatever the module template generates for your Android Studio version rather than copying test library versions from a book, as these move independently.

The fix: configure the app build type

The next step is to ensure the target app module includes a matching benchmark build type. This build type must be a copy of the release build but signed with the debug key. This allows it to install on your test device without requiring your upload key, while still retaining the optimizations and lack of debug instrumentation found in the release variant.

Add the following configuration to your app module's build.gradle.kts:

// app/build.gradle.kts
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true
            isShrinkResources = true
            proguardFiles(
                getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
                "proguard-rules.pro")
        }
        create("benchmark") {
            initWith(getByName("release"))
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
            matchingFallbacks += listOf("release")
        }
    }
}

This configuration ensures that when you run Macrobenchmark, it installs the app using the benchmark build type. This variant inherits isMinifyEnabled and isShrinkResources from release, meaning code is obfuscated and resources are shrunk. It also includes the `` tag, which Android Studio's Benchmark module template creates automatically. This tag tells the system to expose performance data without adding the overhead of full debug instrumentation.

The fix: use Macrobenchmark for user experience metrics

Once your build types are configured, you can use Jetpack Macrobenchmark to measure what users actually experience. Macrobenchmark drives interactions like app startup, scrolling, animations, and navigation from a separate test module. It installs the app, controls compilation, kills and restarts it, and runs your interaction many times. It reports metrics such as time to initial display and frame durations, plus a Perfetto trace of every iteration.

The book provides a table that maps questions to tools. For "How long does startup take, really?" and "Does scrolling drop frames?", the correct tool is Macrobenchmark combined with StartupTimingMetric or FrameTimingMetric. For "Where did the time go?", you should use a Perfetto trace generated by Macrobenchmark or the profiler. If you are asking "Is this one function slow?", you might consider Microbenchmark, but only after a trace has shown that a specific function matters. Most startup and jank problems are not about one hot function, so Macrobenchmark is the right first tool for release-like builds.

Checklist

  • Verify your macrobenchmark module uses the com.android.test plugin.
  • Ensure the app module has a benchmark build type that inherits from release.
  • Confirm the benchmark build type uses the debug signing config.
  • Check that the app includes the `` tag via the Android Studio template.
  • Use Macrobenchmark for startup, scrolling, and animation metrics on release-like builds.
  • Reserve Layout Inspector for finding recomposition issues in debug builds only.
  • Use Microbenchmark only after traces identify specific slow functions.
  • Take dependency versions from the module template rather than copying fixed versions.

item.title: Trunk, access, PVID: the only VLAN words that matter
item.description: Stop guessing about switch ports. Learn how to configure tagged trunks and untagged access ports correctly to isolate IoT, trusted, and guest networks from day one.
item.content:encoded:
Most new home lab builders size their VLAN strategy for the devices they have today. That is the trap. A single desktop computer looks fine on a generic network, so a flat setup feels generous on day one, and nothing about it looks wrong until a smart plug or a guest device quietly compromises the entire segment.

The book Lock Down Your Home Network opens its networking chapter with exactly this, under a heading that sums it up: VLANs from the Wire Up. This post covers the three words that fix it—trunk, access, and PVID—and why leaving VLAN 1 active is a critical failure. It explains how to map physical cables to logical networks so that separation is real, not cosmetic.

One caveat, straight from the book: this guidance assumes you are using a managed switch and a firewall capable of routing multiple interfaces. If your hardware does not support tagging, these steps will not apply. Always check your switch manual for specific menu names, as the logic remains the same even if the clicks differ.

The trap: assuming ports just work

VLANs fail in one of two ways. Either the tag never makes it from the firewall to the device, because a switch port or hypervisor bridge strips it, leaving the device on the wrong network. Or the tag is optional where it should not be, allowing a port that should only carry IoT traffic to also accept the trusted network. Both failures come from not knowing which port is tagged, which is untagged, and why.

The IEEE 802.1Q standard adds a 4-byte tag to each Ethernet frame. Inside that tag is a 12-bit VLAN ID, meaning IDs run from 1 to 4094. A switch uses these tags to keep traffic separate. When a frame leaves through a port belonging to one VLAN only, the switch removes the tag so the end device sees plain Ethernet. Understanding this mechanism is the difference between isolation and chaos.

The fix: trunk, access, and PVID

Every switch port falls into one of two categories. An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN. Frames leave without a tag and arrive without one. The switch assigns incoming frames to the port's VLAN, often called the PVID or native VLAN. You use these for ordinary devices like TVs, printers, and desktops that do not understand tagging.

A trunk port carries several VLANs. Each frame is tagged with its ID as it travels between network devices that understand tags. You use trunks between the firewall and switch, switch to switch, switch to access point, or switch to a virtualization host like Proxmox.

The critical rule for trunks is that they can carry one VLAN untagged. Keep that untagged VLAN to the management VLAN or nothing at all. Never leave VLAN 1, the default on almost every switch, carrying anything you care about. If a port is an access port, it must be removed from VLAN 1 entirely to prevent accidental leakage.

The setup: firewall, switch, and guests

Start with an address plan. Write down your VLANs, names, subnets, and DHCP ranges in a table. For example, VLAN 10 for TRUSTED at 192.168.10.0/24, VLAN 30 for IOT at 192.168.30.0/24, and VLAN 99 for MGMT at 192.168.99.0/24. Keep this table next to your switch while you configure it.

On the firewall, create a VLAN device for each network. Set the parent interface to the physical port connecting to the switch, set the tag to the VLAN ID, and assign an IP address. Enable the interface and configure DHCP ranges where needed. By default, OPNsense blocks all traffic on new interfaces until you add rules, which is the correct secure starting point.

On the managed switch, configure the ports based on their role. The port to the firewall must be a member of all five VLANs, tagged. The port to an access point should carry the wireless VLANs (like 10, 30, and 40) tagged, plus VLAN 99 untagged if the access point uses it for management. Ports to ordinary wired devices must be untagged members of exactly one VLAN and removed from VLAN 1.

For virtualization, if you use Proxmox, ensure the bridge is VLAN-aware. In /etc/network/interfaces, set bridge-vlan-aware yes and define the VLAN IDs. Connect the firewall VM with no VLAN tag on its network card so it receives all tagged frames, while ordinary guests receive a specific tag on their virtual NICs.

The wireless layer: SSIDs and isolation

Wireless networks require one SSID per zone. Map each Wi-Fi name to its corresponding VLAN ID. For instance, "Home" maps to VLAN 10, and "Home-IoT" maps to VLAN 30. On the guest network, enable client isolation, sometimes called AP isolation or guest mode. This prevents guest devices from reaching each other on the same access point, a restriction the firewall cannot enforce because that traffic never leaves the access point.

Be aware that many IoT devices only speak 2.4 GHz and may dislike WPA3 or band steering. If a device fails to join, configure the IoT network for 2.4 GHz with WPA2 rather than weakening the security of your trusted network. This keeps the secure zone robust while accommodating older hardware.

Checklist: VLANs

  • Address plan table written, third octet matching the VLAN ID
  • VLAN devices created on the right parent, assigned, enabled, addressed
  • DHCP running on each network that needs it
  • Switch: trunk to firewall, access point and hosts; access ports for devices
  • VLAN 1 removed from every port that does not need it
  • One SSID per wireless zone, tagged; client isolation on guest
  • Proxmox bridge VLAN-aware; firewall NIC untagged, guests tagged
  • A test device on each VLAN gets the right address from the right range

item.title: Luma OS is in alpha. Start with a VM.
item.description: What Luma is, how to try it without replacing your operating system, and what the Earshot and Hartmann Office build shows about making apps for it.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re curious about Luma, don’t start by replacing the OS on the computer you depend on. Start with a virtual machine. Luma is a free, open-source operating system designed to span computers, tablets and phones. The Try Luma tool lets you explore it from a Mac, Windows or Linux computer while leaving your existing system in place.

What “alpha” means here

The Luma team calls this an alpha. Different devices and apps can be at different stages. Treat a successful test in one VM as evidence for that VM, not a compatibility guarantee for your laptop, phone or tablet. Keep important files in your host system and stick to test data on your first pass. Use Luma’s download page if you’re considering a native install, and check the instructions for your specific device first.

A first session that tells you something

  1. Open Try Luma on your current computer and start the virtual environment. Write down the guest build and architecture when you test something you may want to try again later.
  2. Open Depot, Luma’s app catalog, and try an app already listed there. For a GitHub Flatpak, use the release notes and match the package to the guest architecture. Don’t assume a Depot draft is an install link.
  3. Pick one real task with disposable data: play a podcast episode or edit a small document. Close and reopen the app and see what it remembers. That’s a better check than simply seeing a window open.

Two apps we’ve been building for it

Earshot is a podcast player with direct RSS, a queue and saved playback position. In our original x86_64 Luma VM, we used it to follow Homelab the Right Way, play an episode, and reopen the same episode at the saved position. That’s a guest test; it doesn’t tell us how Bluetooth or playback behaves on every device.

Hartmann Office has local document, spreadsheet and slide editors. It uses OpenDocument files and is built for Luma’s interface. Both projects have public GitHub releases you can reach from our Apps page. We checked that the newer ARM packages import; we’re not calling that an ARM device test, or calling either app available in Depot.

item.title: Home Assistant Without Regret: A Setup Guide
item.description: Avoid common pitfalls in Home Assistant deployment by choosing the right install method, securing backups, bridging MQTT brokers, cleaning stale automations, and configuring safe remote access.
item.content:encoded:
Home Assistant tends to become the most important thing in your lab without anyone deciding it should. It runs the lights, the thermostat, and the garage door. When it breaks, the household notices before you do. Treat it like production from day one to avoid regret later.

The book opens this chapter by highlighting four ways to install Home Assistant, noting that they are not equal. Many users fall into the trap of choosing a method that lacks long-term support or flexibility, only to find themselves maintaining deprecated software or managing complex dependencies manually. This guide covers the correct installation paths, how to back up data that actually survives disasters, how to bridge MQTT brokers without creating loops, how to clean out stale automations, and how to reach your instance safely from outside.

The trap: choosing a deprecated install method

The first trap is picking an installation method that the Home Assistant project no longer supports for new releases. There are four ways to run Home Assistant, and they carry different levels of risk and maintenance overhead.

Home Assistant OS in a VM is the recommended approach, particularly on Proxmox. It provides full Supervisor access, add-ons, one-click backups, and updates. The Container (Docker) method is fine if you are comfortable running add-on equivalents yourself, such as Mosquitto, Z-Wave JS, and others, as separate containers.

However, Core (a Python virtual environment) and Supervised were deprecated by the Home Assistant project in 2025. They are no longer supported for new releases. If you are on a Core install, you must plan a migration. The caveats pile up quickly: there are no add-ons, every Home Assistant release may require a newer Python than your OS ships, dependency builds break during upgrades, and you are on your own for backups of everything outside the config folder.

The move is straightforward but requires care. Make a full backup from the Core install by navigating to Settings → System → Backups. Stand up a Home Assistant OS VM, and restore that backup during onboarding. Keep the old instance shut down, not deleted, for a couple of weeks to ensure stability before decommissioning it.

The trap: storing backups in the same place

A backup stored on the same VM as Home Assistant protects you from a bad update. It does not protect you from a dead disk, a ransomware infection, or a house fire. You want three copies: the live system, a local backup, and one off-site.

Recent Home Assistant versions have automatic backups built in. Go to Settings → System → Backups, choose a schedule, how many to keep, and where to put them. Locations include network storage, which you must add first under Settings → System → Storage → Add network storage as an SMB or NFS share on your NAS. You can also use Home Assistant Cloud, which stores an encrypted backup off-site for subscribers. Additionally, add-ons and integrations for Google Drive, OneDrive, and others appear as extra backup locations.

Watch out for the encryption key. Home Assistant encrypts automatic backups with an emergency key. Download that key and store it in your password manager. Without it, an off-site backup is a very securely locked brick.

The Proxmox side helps too. The nightly vzdump of the Home Assistant VM gives you a whole-machine restore point. But that copy usually lives on the same NAS, so it isn't off-site. Pick one copy to send off-site; rclone to cloud storage from the NAS works well. Check it monthly to ensure the data is intact and accessible.

The trap: creating MQTT bridge loops

MQTT is the glue for a lot of home automation, including Zigbee2MQTT, ESPHome alternatives, custom scripts, and integrations from other systems. When you have more than one broker, such as Home Assistant's Mosquitto add-on and a separate broker on a container that a script publishes to, bridge them instead of pointing everything at one fragile box.

A Mosquitto bridge config on the sending broker looks like this:

# /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/bridge.conf
connection ha-bridge
address 10.30.0.30:1883
remote_username bridge_user
remote_password <use-a-long-random-password>
cleansession false
restart_timeout 10 30
# Topic pattern, direction, QoS, local prefix, remote prefix
topic sensors/# out 1 "" ""
topic commands/# in 1 "" ""

Things that trip people up include direction and retained messages. Direction is from the bridge's point of view. out sends local messages to the remote broker; in pulls remote messages down; both does both. Using both with the same topics on two bridges creates a loop. Retained messages and discovery can also cause confusion. If you bridge Home Assistant's homeassistant/# discovery topics, retained config messages copy across. That is useful once, but confusing when you delete a device and it keeps coming back. Clear a retained topic with mosquitto_pub -t -r -n.

Authentication is critical. Never run a broker with allow_anonymous true on a network other devices can reach. You can watch the state of bridges using mosquitto_sub -v -t '$SYS/broker/connection/#', and prove data is flowing by running mosquitto_sub -v -t 'sensors/#' on the far side.

The trap: letting stale automations accumulate

Over a couple of years, automations accumulate. You get ones for devices you no longer own, duplicates you made while experimenting, and ones that reference entities that were renamed. They clutter the UI, log errors, and occasionally fire at the worst moment.

Settings → Repairs catches some of this. For the rest, paste these into Developer Tools → Template to find automations that have never triggered:

{# Automations that have never triggered #}
{{ states.automation
   | selectattr('attributes.last_triggered', 'none')
   | map(attribute='entity_id') | list }}

You can also find entities that are unavailable right now:

{# Entities that are unavailable right now #}
{{ states | selectattr('state', 'eq', 'unavailable')
   | map(attribute='entity_id') | list }}

Cross-reference these lists. An automation that has never fired and mentions an unavailable entity is a deletion candidate. Before deleting, disable it for two weeks. If nobody notices, delete it. If your automations live in YAML, commit the folder to git first, so "delete" is never permanent.

The trap: exposing port 8123 directly

Do not port-forward 8123 to the internet. Use Tailscale (covered in the next chapter), Home Assistant Cloud, or a reverse proxy behind a tunnel with strong authentication. If you use a reverse proxy, you must add its address under trusted_proxies in configuration.yaml, or Home Assistant will reject the forwarded requests.

The configuration looks like this:

http:
  use_x_forwarded_for: true
  trusted_proxies:
    - 10.30.0.40      # your reverse proxy

Checklist

  • Running Home Assistant OS (VM) or Container, not Core or Supervised
  • Automatic backups on a schedule, with retention
  • One copy off-site; emergency key saved in your password manager
  • MQTT brokers authenticated; bridges with explicit topic directions
  • Stale automations disabled, then deleted after two quiet weeks
  • No 8123 port-forward; remote access through Tailscale, Cloud or an authenticated proxy

item.title: Hartmann Office: documents, spreadsheets and slides on Luma
item.description: An open-source office suite for Luma, with local files, OpenDocument support and no account required to edit.
item.content:encoded:
A quick meeting note, a parts budget and a five-slide walkthrough don’t need three separate apps. Hartmann Office bundles a document editor, a spreadsheet and a presentation editor for Luma. The editors work with local files and don’t require an account. Open the app and you can start working without signing into a cloud service.

Three editors, one file library

Use Documents for notes and reports: headings, lists, basic formatting, word count, find and replace, and Letter or A4 pages. For a small project budget, Spreadsheets gives you multiple sheets, familiar functions like SUM, IF and VLOOKUP, number formatting, sorting and fill down. Presentations is for simple decks: title and section slides, themes, speaker notes and a full-screen presentation mode.

Try a small workflow before moving anything important. Make a one-page plan, total a few parts in a sheet, and build a three-slide status update. Save copies, reopen them, and check how the layout looks in the editor the recipient actually uses.

Use OpenDocument when you share

Hartmann Office uses .odt, .ods and .odp for documents, sheets and slides. That gives you a starting point for sharing with LibreOffice or other apps that support OpenDocument. It isn’t a promise that complex files will look identical in every editor. If the other person only needs to read or print the result, PDF is the safer handoff. There’s also support for CSV and Markdown where those simpler formats make sense.

Free editors, optional Pro

The three editors are free to use. Office Pro adds extras such as document and slide templates, more themes, version history, and headers, footers and page numbering on printed or exported documents. The app source, including the Pro code, is published under GPL-3.0-or-later. Buying Pro is optional, and Stripe handles payments separately from your files.

Try the public build

Use the Hartmann Office GitHub release for the public Flatpak packages and checksums. This isn’t a Depot install. Our newer 1.2.1 build was tested on the x86_64 Luma VM; ARM package import passed, but that’s not the same as testing on an ARM device. If you find an OpenDocument compatibility issue, a small example that doesn’t include private data is useful in the Hartmann Office repository.

If you haven’t tried Luma yet, start with the Luma VM guide. You can also find Hartmann Office and Earshot together on our Apps page.

item.title: Earshot: a podcast player built for Luma
item.description: Follow podcasts by RSS, pick up where you left off, and take your listening queue offline with Earshot, an open-source player for Luma.
item.content:encoded:
A podcast player should make it easy to do two things: find a show and come back to the episode you were halfway through. Earshot is our open-source player for Luma. You can browse charts from Apple’s public podcast directory, search for a show, or paste its RSS feed directly. You don’t have to create an Earshot account to listen.

From an RSS link to a listening queue

A practical first test: add the Homelab the Right Way RSS feed, follow the show, and open “Docker on Proxmox — The Official Way & Anatomy of a Compose”. Pasting RSS is useful when a directory search doesn’t turn up the exact show. That’s what happened in our VM test: search returned results, but the feed link was the direct way to the show. We streamed the episode, paused and resumed it, then reopened Earshot and saw the episode at the saved spot.

Up Next lets you line up episodes in order. The player supports pitch-preserving speed changes, chapters when the feed includes them, and a sleep timer. Download an episode before going offline. If you’re switching podcast apps, OPML import and export let you move your subscription list instead of following every show again.

What’s free, and what’s optional

Discovery, following, queueing, downloads and regular playback are part of the free player. Earshot Plus adds extras such as voice boost, per-show intro and outro skipping, and automatic downloads for selected shows. There are no ads or required app accounts. Listening history and the library are kept on your device; directory searches go to the directory provider, and fetching feeds and audio connects to their hosts. Optional purchases and restores use purchase records and email; payments are handled by Stripe.

Try the public build

Start with Earshot’s public GitHub release. Pick the asset that matches the Luma system you’re running, not necessarily the processor in your host computer. The release page has the Flatpak bundles and checksums. This is the public GitHub build, not a Depot install. The newer 1.2.1 package was exercised in our x86_64 Luma VM; the ARM package passed an import check, not a device run.

New to the OS? Read the Luma VM guide or see both Luma apps. For an issue with a feed, the player or the install, use the Earshot repository and include your Luma build, package version and what you were trying to do.

item.title: Avoid SMR drives and RAID cards in ZFS homelabs
item.description: Learn why hardware RAID controllers and SMR hard drives destroy ZFS performance and reliability, and how to use HBAs, CMR disks, and persistent names instead.
item.content:encoded:
Most new homelab builders focus on CPU benchmarks or network throughput, assuming that raw disk speed is the final bottleneck. That is the trap. A pool built on a hardware RAID volume, or on SMR drives bought because they were the biggest for the money, using /dev/sda-style names, works for months. Then a disk fails, the RAID card reports "optimal" while ZFS sees checksum errors it cannot repair, the resilver onto the new drive crawls for days, and after a reboot the pool imports with a different disk in slot sdb.

The book Store It Right opens its first chapter on hardware with exactly this warning. This post covers the three critical hardware decisions that determine whether your ZFS pool survives long-term: choosing the right controller interface, selecting the correct drive technology, and naming disks persistently.

The trap: trusting a hardware RAID card

A hardware RAID controller presents a virtual disk to the operating system. ZFS then sees one big "drive" and cannot tell which physical disk returned bad data, cannot repair it from parity it does not control, and cannot read SMART data through most RAID firmware. The card's write cache can also acknowledge writes that are not on disk yet, which undoes ZFS's careful write ordering.

The book explains that a RAID card hides the disks behind one virtual volume, so ZFS can detect corruption but not fix it. An HBA in IT mode passes every disk straight through, so ZFS sees each drive, its serial number and SMART data. What ZFS wants is an HBA (host bus adapter): a controller that simply connects disks. The common homelab choice is a used LSI/Broadcom SAS card of the 9300 series class running IT mode (initiator-target) firmware, which turns off all RAID logic.

Many cards sold for servers ship in IR (RAID) mode; some can be cross-flashed to IT firmware. The procedure differs by card and firmware generation and can brick a card if done wrong, so check your card's documentation and the vendor's firmware notes before flashing anything.

WATCH OUT "JBOD mode" or "passthrough mode" on a RAID card is not the same as IT mode. Some cards still hide SMART data or reorder writes in those modes. If you cannot see each disk's serial number with smartctl -i (Chapter 7), ZFS cannot see the disk properly either.

Motherboard SATA ports are fine for ZFS when the pool lives on the host itself. You only need a separate HBA when you run out of ports or when you want to pass all the disks to a TrueNAS VM in one piece.

The trap: buying SMR drives for capacity

Hard drives record data in two ways. CMR (conventional magnetic recording) writes tracks side by side. SMR (shingled magnetic recording) overlaps tracks like roof shingles to fit more data, which means rewriting one track forces the drive to rewrite its neighbours. SMR drives hide this behind a cache, which is fine for occasional writes and terrible for long sustained ones.

CMR tracks sit side by side and can be rewritten one at a time. SMR tracks overlap, so a sustained rewrite (a resilver, a scrub repair, a big copy) fills the drive's cache and throughput collapses. A resilver is exactly that workload: hours of sustained writes to one disk. SMR drives can slow a resilver from hours to days, and a long resilver is the window in which a second failure loses data. Use CMR drives for every ZFS pool. Manufacturers list the recording technology in their datasheets; check the exact model number, because the same product family can include both.

The book provides a clear guide for interface selection:

InterfaceGood forWatch out for

| SAS HDD | The same, with dual ports and better error reporting | Needs a SAS HBA or backplane; often louder |

| SATA SSD | Boot mirror, small fast pools, special vdevs | Consumer drives without power-loss protection |

| NVMe SSD | VM disks, databases, a fast mirror pool | Heat; limited M.2 slots; PCIe lanes on small boards |

A typical homelab NAS ends up with two pools: a mirror of SSDs or NVMe drives for VM disks and containers, and a pool of large hard drives for everything else. Keep them separate; mixing fast and slow disks in one pool makes it as slow as its slowest vdev.

The trap: using /dev/sda names

Linux hands out /dev/sda, /dev/sdb in the order disks are detected, and that order can change when you add a controller or a disk is slow to spin up. Persistent names live in /dev/disk/by-id/ and include the model and serial number, which is also what is printed on the drive's label.

The book advises building every pool with these names. When a disk fails, zpool status then tells you the serial number of the drive to pull, and you never have to guess which sdX it was. You can verify your disk IDs using the following commands:

ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/ | grep -v part
# ata-WDC_WD80EFPX-68C4ZN0_WD-RD1ABC12 -> ../../sda
# ata-WDC_WD80EFPX-68C4ZN0_WD-RD1ABC34 -> ../../sdb
# nvme-Samsung_SSD_990_PRO_2TB_S7DNNJ0X123456A -> ../../nvme0n1
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,SERIAL,ROTA

TIP Write the last four characters of each serial number on a label stuck to the front of the drive bay. Ten seconds of labelling now saves pulling the wrong disk from a degraded pool later.

Passing an HBA through to a VM

For the TrueNAS-in-a-VM design, the VM must own the disk controller outright. Proxmox does this with PCI(e) passthrough, documented in the Proxmox VE admin guide. The steps, in order:

  1. Enable IOMMU (Intel VT-d or AMD-Vi) and virtualization in the firmware setup.
  2. On AMD CPUs IOMMU is on by default; on Intel it is on by default with kernel 6.8 or newer, which is what Proxmox VE 9 ships. Older kernels need intel_iommu=on on the kernel command line.
  3. Load the VFIO modules at boot and refresh the initramfs.
  4. Check that the HBA sits in its own IOMMU group.
  5. Add the device to the VM.
# Confirm the IOMMU is on
dmesg | grep -e DMAR -e IOMMU
# Load VFIO at boot
printf 'vfio\nvfio_iommu_type1\nvfio_pci\n' > /etc/modules-load.d/vfio.conf
update-initramfs -u -k all
reboot
# After the reboot
lsmod | grep vfio
lspci -nn | grep -i -e LSI -e SAS
pvesh get /nodes/$(hostname)/hardware/pci --pci-class-blacklist ""

Checklist

  • Replace any hardware RAID controller with an LSI/Broadcom SAS card of the 9300 series class running IT mode firmware, ensuring it is flashed correctly according to vendor documentation.
  • Verify that your HBA is in true IT mode and not a "JBOD" or "passthrough" mode that still hides SMART data or reorders writes.
  • Select only CMR drives for bulk storage pools, checking datasheets for the exact model number to avoid SMR variants that collapse during resilvers.
  • Use persistent names from /dev/disk/by-id/ when creating ZFS pools, never relying on /dev/sdX device nodes that can shift after reboots.
  • Label the last four characters of each drive's serial number on the physical bay for quick identification during failures.
  • Enable IOMMU in firmware and load VFIO modules at boot if passing an HBA through to a TrueNAS VM via PCI passthrough.
  • Ensure the HBA resides in its own IOMMU group before adding it to the VM, avoiding ACS overrides unless absolutely necessary.
  • Export any ZFS pools on the host before starting the VM that owns the HBA, preventing simultaneous access and potential corruption.

item.title: Median of 32 reads: taming noisy analog probes
item.description: Learn how the firmware uses median filtering on 32 samples to reject noise spikes from pumps and lamps, ensuring stable TDS and turbidity readings.
item.content:encoded:
Most new homelab builders assume that a single reading from an analog probe is accurate enough for their monitoring dashboard. That is the trap. Analog sensors connected to water or air often suffer from electrical noise caused by nearby equipment like filter pumps and lamp timers. A single spike in voltage can skew your data, making it look like a sudden change in water quality when it is just interference.

The book opens its firmware chapter with exactly this problem under the heading reading the probes. It explains that taking one reading is risky, so the firmware takes 32 samples and keeps the median. This post covers why the median works better than an average, how to configure the PlatformIO project for the XIAO board, and the exact code structure used to clean the data before sending it to your server.

One caveat, straight from the book: this is general guidance for the specific hardware outlined in Chapter 3 (the Seeed XIAO ESP32 C3). Your board may have different pin mappings or ADC characteristics, so check every number against your own hardware.

The trap: letting spikes skew your average

The usual way people find out their analog readings are noisy is that the graph shows sudden, impossible jumps. If you calculate a simple average of 32 random samples, one massive spike can pull the entire result up or down significantly. The book’s answer is to use the median instead of the mean for analog pins.

The firmware reads one sensor at a time, takes 32 samples, and keeps the middle value. This approach ensures that a single spike in the data stream cannot skew the final reading. The filter pump and the lamp timer are where these spikes usually come from. By sorting the 32 values and picking the center, you throw out the outliers that an average would otherwise include.

To implement this, you need to set up your PlatformIO environment correctly. The project configuration in platformio.ini must match the XIAO board exactly:

[env:xiao_c3]
platform = espressif32
board = seeed_xiao_esp32c3
framework = arduino
monitor_speed = 115200
build_flags =
  -DARDUINO_USB_MODE=1
  -DARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=1
lib_deps =
  paulstoffregen/OneWire
  milesburton/DallasTemperature
  bblanchon/ArduinoJson@^7

The board = seeed_xiao_esp32c3 line picks the pin names like D1, D2, and D4. If you use a different board name, those letters map to different physical pins. The monitor_speed = 115200 sets the serial speed; if your monitor shows garbage characters, this number disagrees with Serial.begin() in the code. The two build_flags enable USB CDC so you can watch readings via the USB-C port without extra drivers.

The fix: median filtering in code

The core of the noise reduction lies in a small function that handles the analog pins. It takes 32 readings, sorts them, and returns the middle value. Here is the exact implementation from the book:

static float medianMv(int pin) {     // 32 reads, keep the median
    uint16_t v[32];
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) { v[i] = analogReadMilliVolts(pin); delay(10); }
    std::sort(v, v + 32);
    return (v[15] + v[16]) / 2.0f;
}

This function uses analogReadMilliVolts(), which applies the chip’s factory calibration and returns millivolts instead of raw counts. This is accurate up to about 2.5 V at the default attenuation. The delay(10) spaces the reads 10 milliseconds apart, totaling about a third of a second for the full set. The sort is what makes it a median; without it, you would just be averaging noisy data.

You must also define the pins correctly in your code to ensure you are reading from the right GPIOs:

#define TEMP_PIN D4        // GPIO6, DS18B20 DAT (adapter has the pull-up)
#define TDS_PIN D1         // GPIO3, ADC1
#define TURB_PIN D2        // GPIO4, ADC1, through the /5 divider module
#define TURB_RATIO 5.0f    // 2.0f if you used the two-resistor divider

Both analog pins are on ADC1, which matters on an ESP32 because ADC2 stops working while Wi-Fi is active. ADC1 does not have this limitation. If you built a different voltage divider for the turbidity sensor, adjust TURB_RATIO accordingly (e.g., 2.0f) to undo the signal shrinking before it reaches the pin.

The trap: reading probes in parallel or during network calls

Another common mistake is trying to read multiple probes at the same time or reading them while sending data over HTTPS. The book warns that reading TDS and turbidity probes together can make the TDS number jumpy because they both put a small voltage into the same water. Sequential reads fix most of this issue.

Furthermore, you should never read probes inside the send function to "get fresh numbers." A failed TLS handshake can take 15 seconds, and if your watchdog is set to 90 seconds, the reading cadence becomes dependent on network stability. Instead, keep sampling and sending on separate timers.

The main loop in the firmware handles this separation cleanly:

void loop() {
    esp_task_wdt_reset();
    uint32_t now = millis();
    if (now - lastSample >= SAMPLE_MS) { lastSample = now; sampleOnce(); }
    if (now - lastSend >= sendEveryMs) {
        lastSend = now;
        pushReading();
        if (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) connectWifi();
        if (WiFi.status() == WL_CONNECTED && sendBuffered()) failures = 0;
        else if (++failures >= 8) ESP.restart();
    }
    delay(200);
}

The first if runs sampleOnce() every SAMPLE_MS (30 seconds), using millis() arithmetic that survives the 49-day rollover. The second if handles the sending interval. This structure ensures that network issues do not delay your sensor readings.

Checklist

  • Verify board = seeed_xiao_esp32c3 in platformio.ini matches your hardware.
  • Set monitor_speed = 115200 to avoid garbage serial output.
  • Use analogReadMilliVolts() for ADC1 pins to get calibrated millivolt values.
  • Implement the medianMv function to sort 32 samples and return the middle value.
  • Define TURB_RATIO correctly based on your voltage divider (5.0f or 2.0f).
  • Keep sampling and sending on separate timers in the main loop.
  • Reject DS18B20 values of -127°C and 85.0°C as invalid readings.
  • Reset the watchdog with esp_task_wdt_reset() to prevent wedged reboots.

item.title: PBS Maintenance: Prune, GC, and Verify Jobs
item.description: Proxmox Backup Server requires three specific maintenance jobs to stay healthy. Learn how to schedule prune, garbage collection, and verify tasks to ensure data integrity and free up space.
item.content:encoded:
Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) is designed to replace vzdump by splitting disks into chunks and storing each unique chunk only once. This approach means that after the initial full backup, subsequent nightly runs for a small daily change set take minutes rather than hours. However, this efficiency comes with a maintenance burden that many users overlook until space runs out or corruption is discovered.

The trap is assuming that PBS manages itself automatically. It does not. You must explicitly schedule three specific jobs on the datastore: prune, garbage collection, and verify. Without these, your backups will eventually become unmanageable in size or silently corrupt. The book emphasizes that while verification is necessary, it is not sufficient on its own; you need a complete maintenance routine to keep the system healthy.

Prune jobs: dropping old snapshots

Pruning is the process of removing old backup snapshots from the index. When you configure retention policies, such as keeping daily backups for seven days and weekly backups for four weeks, PBS needs to know when to stop tracking those older entries. If you do not set up prune jobs, the index grows indefinitely, and the datastore fills up with references to data that is no longer useful.

You must set the same keep-* numbers in your prune job configuration that you chose in your retention policy. For example, if you want to retain seven daily backups, the prune job should reflect that constraint. This job runs on a schedule to clean up the metadata, ensuring that the datastore does not waste space holding onto expired backup entries.

Garbage collection: freeing actual disk space

Pruning only removes the index entries; it does not free the actual data blocks on disk. That is where garbage collection (GC) comes in. GC scans the datastore and deletes chunks that are no longer referenced by any remaining snapshot. However, PBS protects recently deleted data with a grace period to prevent accidental loss during restoration windows. By default, this grace period is 24 hours and 5 minutes.

If you run prune but never run garbage collection, your datastore will appear full even though the index says there is plenty of space. The book advises scheduling garbage collection daily. You should expect that free space will lag behind pruning by about a day because GC waits for the grace period to expire before deleting chunks. This delay is intentional and ensures you can still restore backups created within the last 24 hours even after they have been pruned from the index.

Verify jobs: checking data integrity

Verification reads every chunk in the datastore and checks its hash against the stored metadata. This process detects silent corruption, such as bit rot on a hard drive, that might otherwise go unnoticed until you attempt a restore. Because verification is disk-heavy and can impact performance, it should be scheduled during a quiet time, such as early morning.

The recommended configuration for verify jobs is to run them weekly. You should enable the "skip verified" option, which prevents PBS from re-checking chunks that have already been validated within the current window. Additionally, set "re-verify after" to 30 days. This ensures that every chunk is checked at least once a month, balancing thoroughness with resource usage.

Why vzdump alone is not enough

While vzdump creates full or incremental copies of entire guests, PBS offers deduplication across guests and file-level restores from any backup directly through the Proxmox GUI. However, these advanced features rely on the integrity of the chunk store. If you skip maintenance, the chunk store degrades. Pruning without garbage collection wastes space. Garbage collection without pruning is inefficient. Verification without a schedule leaves corruption undetected.

The book notes that PBS also supports sync jobs to another PBS instance for off-site copies and namespaces for multi-cluster setups. It even allows host backups using proxmox-backup-client to back up plain directories like /etc. All these features depend on a healthy datastore, which is maintained exclusively through the three jobs described above.

Checklist

  • Schedule prune jobs with the same keep-* numbers as your retention policy
  • Run garbage collection daily and expect free space to lag pruning by one day
  • Configure weekly verify jobs with "skip verified" enabled and "re-verify after" set to 30 days
  • Ensure PBS runs on its own hardware or dedicated disks, not on the same pool as the host
  • Use a backup@pbs user with DatastoreBackup permissions for Proxmox nodes
  • Save the client-side encryption key outside the cluster immediately after setup
  • Back up the Proxmox hosts' /etc and /etc/pve using proxmox-backup-client

item.title: Trap: Indecision Costs a Rewrite
item.description: Adding ads and purchases without a clear model creates cluttered free tiers and confused store listings. This guide explains how to pick one model using four questions before writing code.
item.content:encoded:
Most new Android developers treat the business model as an afterthought. They add AdMob "for now" and promise a purchase "later," assuming they can sort out the payments logic once the code works. That is the trap. The result is an app whose free version is either so generous nobody pays or so cluttered nobody stays, a purchase that nobody can describe in one sentence, and a store listing that cannot honestly say what the user gets. Changing the model after launch is possible but expensive: users who installed a free app do not enjoy discovering a paywall, and an app that sold a lifetime unlock cannot easily turn that into a subscription. Ten minutes of deciding now saves a rewrite later.

The book opens its first chapter with exactly this warning under the heading "Pick a Business Model Before You Write Code." It argues that the business model decides your dependencies, your consent obligations, your Data safety answers, your store listing wording and whether you need a server. This post covers the five common models, the four questions to help you choose, and the one-paragraph statement you must write before adding any SDKs.

The trap: mixing models without a plan

The usual way people fall into this trap is by combining ads and purchases without defining the boundary between them. You might think that showing ads and offering a remove-ads purchase is simple, but the book notes that "most small apps end up as 'ads plus a remove-ads purchase', which is two models in one." This hybrid approach needs both halves done properly. If you do not decide what the free experience is upfront, you risk creating an app where the free tier feels like a trap or the paid tier offers no clear value. The book states that the result of this indecision is an app whose free version is either so generous nobody pays or so cluttered nobody stays. You must define the boundary before writing code, not after.

The five models compared

Before choosing, you need to understand what each model requires in terms of user payment, backend work, and disclosure. The book lists five common models:

  • Paid app. The user pays once on Google Play before installing. There is nothing to build in the app, but the listing has to sell the app without a trial.
  • Free with ads. The app is free and shows AdMob ads. You need the ads SDK, a consent flow (Chapter 3) and honest ad placement (Chapter 4).
  • One-time unlock. The app is free and a single in-app purchase unlocks a feature set or removes ads permanently. You need Play Billing (Chapters 5 and 6).
  • Subscription. The user pays on a recurring schedule for continuing value: content, sync, a hosted service. You need Play Billing, a way to handle renewals, holds and cancellations, and in practice a backend (Chapter 7).
  • Hybrid. Ads for free users plus a purchase or subscription that removes them. This is what most small utilities do. It needs both halves.

Most developers gravitate toward the hybrid model because it seems to capture both casual and power users. However, the book warns that this requires implementing two distinct revenue streams correctly. If you choose a paid app, you avoid backend complexity but must convince users to pay upfront. If you choose a subscription, you accept recurring billing complexity and likely need a server.

The four questions to decide

The book provides a decision framework consisting of four questions, asked in order. The first "yes" usually decides the model. If the answer to all four is "no," a free app with a few well-placed ads and a remove-ads purchase is the honest default. You should ask these questions before writing any code:

  1. Does the app cost you money every time it is used (a server, an API, storage)? Then a subscription matches cost to revenue. A one-time price will eventually be paid off by heavy users and keep costing you.
  2. Is the value one complete thing (a tool that just works)? A paid app or a one-time unlock is simpler for everyone.
  3. Is the audience large and casual (a flashlight, a QR scanner, a timer)? Ads fit, because few people will pay for something they use for ten seconds.
  4. Would ads damage the core use (a journal, a medical log, a focus app)? Then do not use ads at all; sell an unlock or a subscription.

These questions force you to align your technical constraints with user expectations. For example, if your app requires a server that costs money per request, question one dictates a subscription. If your app is a simple utility used for seconds, question three suggests ads are more appropriate than a paywall.

The Google Play Billing requirement

Once you have selected a model involving digital goods, you must comply with Google's Payments policy. The book states that at the time of writing, the policy page in Play Console Help ("Payments") says that apps charging for downloads must use Google Play's billing system, and that in-app purchases of digital features, content or services must use it too (with specific exceptions listed in the policy). The examples it lists include virtual items, subscription services and, word for word, "app functionality or content (such as an ad-free version of app or new features not available in the free version)."

The same page says Play billing must not be used for physical goods, physical services (transport, food delivery, event tickets and similar) and bill payments. So: a remove-ads purchase goes through Play Billing; selling a T-shirt from your app does not. You must read the current policy page before planning anything other than plain Google Play Billing, as regional programs and exceptions come with their own requirements and fees.

The one-paragraph model statement

The final step is to write down your decision in a single paragraph before you start Chapter 2 of the book or begin coding. This statement becomes your consent message settings, your Data safety answers, your paywall text and your store listing's first line. If you cannot write it, you are not ready to add an SDK.

For example: "Free, with a banner on the main list and an interstitial after every third saved item. A one-time Remove Ads purchase removes all ads forever. No other purchases."

Checklist

  • [ ] Answer the four decision questions in order and identify the first "yes."
  • [ ] Select one of the five models (Paid, Free with ads, One-time unlock, Subscription, or Hybrid).
  • [ ] Verify that your chosen model complies with Google Play's Payments policy for digital goods.
  • [ ] Check if you need a backend server for subscriptions or recurring value.
  • [ ] Write a one-paragraph model statement describing the free experience and the paid upgrade.
  • [ ] Ensure your Play developer account is linked to a Google payments profile.
  • [ ] Ship an internal build with the Play Billing Library before configuring products in Play Console.

item.title: Nextcloud or Syncthing? An honest comparison for homelabs
item.description: Decide whether to deploy Nextcloud All-in-One for full suite replacement or use lightweight Syncthing for simple folder sync, avoiding maintenance traps.
item.content:encoded:
Most people size their homelab storage solution for the feature set they admire rather than the workflow they actually use. A fresh Nextcloud installation looks impressive with its calendar, contacts, and document editing suite, so it is easy to assume that full-featured cloud software is the default choice for any file sync task. That assumption is the trap.

If your primary goal is simply keeping a folder identical across your laptop and phone, Nextcloud is a lot of machinery for that job. The honest comparison reveals that while Nextcloud excels as a Google Drive replacement with sharing and collaboration features, Syncthing does the basic sync job better with almost nothing to maintain. Choosing the wrong tool means either over-engineering a simple task or under-serving a complex need.

The trap: the hand-built Nextcloud

The classic way to install Nextcloud involves setting up a web server, PHP, a database, Redis, cron jobs, and a dozen tuning settings by hand. Many tutorials still show this method, but each piece is easy while together they form a full-time hobby. Six months later, a PHP upgrade breaks an app, background jobs stop running weeks ago, and the admin page shows a wall of yellow warnings you have learned to ignore.

This complexity is why the book recommends Nextcloud All-in-One (AIO) if you want a Google Drive replacement. AIO is the official Docker setup maintained by the Nextcloud project, and it runs and updates the whole stack for you. If you only sync a few folders between your own machines, Syncthing does it with almost nothing to maintain. Seafile sits in between and is excellent at large file sync, but it represents a smaller ecosystem than the other two options.

The fix: Nextcloud All-in-One

AIO uses a single mastercontainer that builds and manages the rest of the stack. Since you are putting it behind a reverse proxy, use the reverse-proxy variant of the start command from the AIO documentation. You must not rename the container because AIO self-updates depend on that exact name.

docker run -d --init --sig-proxy=false \
  --name nextcloud-aio-mastercontainer \
  --restart always \
  --publish 8080:8080 \
  --env APACHE_PORT=11000 \
  --env APACHE_IP_BINDING=0.0.0.0 \
  --env APACHE_ADDITIONAL_NETWORK="" \
  --env SKIP_DOMAIN_VALIDATION=false \
  --env NEXTCLOUD_DATADIR=/srv/data/nextcloud \
  --volume nextcloud_aio_mastercontainer:/mnt/docker-aio-config \
  --volume /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
  ghcr.io/nextcloud-releases/all-in-one:latest

Set NEXTCLOUD_DATADIR to put your files on the big data disk. This must be set before the first start because it cannot be changed later without a migration. Moving the data directory after installation is a documented but fiddly process, and getting it wrong is how people lose files.

After starting the container, create a proxy host in Nginx Proxy Manager for cloud.example.com pointing to 192.168.10.20 port 11000, with Websockets Support on and an SSL certificate. Open to accept the self-signed certificate warning once, then copy the passphrase AIO shows you and log in. Enter cloud.example.com` as your domain so AIO checks that the domain reaches it through your proxy. If the check fails, fix the proxy first; do not skip the validation.

Choose the optional containers you want. Collabora for online document editing and Talk are useful but heavy, so start without them and add later. Click Download and start containers and wait, as the first start takes several minutes. AIO shows the initial admin password once, so save it immediately.

The fix: Syncthing for light sync

If you decide that keeping folders identical between devices is all you need, run Syncthing on the Docker VM as one more device that is always on. This ensures your laptop and phone sync through it even when they are never online together.

docker run -d --name syncthing --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8384:8384 -p 22000:22000/tcp -p 22000:22000/udp \
  -p 21027:21027/udp \
  -v /srv/data/syncthing:/var/syncthing \
  syncthing/syncthing:latest

Set a username and password on the web interface at port 8384 the first time you open it. Syncthing is a sync tool, not a backup; if you delete a file on one device, it disappears everywhere. Turn on File Versioning set to Staggered for each shared folder on the server copy to mitigate data loss.

Managing uploads and clients

Replacing Google Drive is half of the job; replacing Google Calendar and Contacts is the other half, and Nextcloud handles both with standard protocols like CalDAV and CardDAV. Enable the Calendar and Contacts apps from the Apps menu in the web interface. For iPhone, go to Settings, select Calendar, then Accounts, choose Add Account, select Other, and add a CalDAV Account using the server cloud.example.com, your Nextcloud username, and an app password created under Personal settings Security. Repeat this with a CardDAV account for contacts.

On Android, install DAVx5, add an account with Login with URL and user name, use the URL and provide the same kind of app password. Export your Google calendars as .ics files and contacts as .vcf` files from Google Takeout, then import them in the Nextcloud web interface. Check a few recurring events and birthdays before you delete anything at Google.

Nginx Proxy Manager limits upload size by default. On the cloud.example.com proxy host, add the following to the Advanced tab to allow larger uploads:

client_max_body_size 0;
proxy_request_buffering off;
proxy_read_timeout 86400s;

Checklist

  • Decide honestly whether you need a Drive replacement or just folder sync
  • Install Nextcloud with AIO rather than building it by hand
  • Set NEXTCLOUD_DATADIR to the data disk before the first start
  • Ensure domain validation passes through your reverse proxy
  • Save the admin password and AIO passphrase in a password manager
  • Configure the proxy to allow large uploads and long timeouts
  • For Syncthing users: set a GUI password and enable staggered file versioning

item.title: ScriptureSearch: find and compare Bible verses across translations
item.description: ScriptureSearch is a free Android app for searching the Bible by keyword or reference, comparing translations and sharing verses.
item.content:encoded:
You remember part of a verse, a phrase or a word, but not where it is. Or you know the reference and want to see how different translations put it. Flipping through a printed Bible or several websites for either job is slow. ScriptureSearch is built for exactly those two moments: find the verse, then compare it.

What it does

  • Search by keyword or reference. Type a word or phrase you remember, or a reference you already know.
  • Compare translations. See how a verse reads in different translations of the Bible.
  • Share verses with friends by social media, email or text.
  • Reading plans and devotionals. The listing mentions access to reading plans and devotionals.
  • Easy to use. A focused app built around search.

Two ways to search

The search box handles both kinds of lookup:

  • Keyword search is for when you remember the words but not the location. Search a distinctive word or short phrase rather than a common one, so the results stay focused.
  • Reference search is for when you know where a verse is and want to read it, or compare it.

A practical habit: when a keyword search turns up too many results, add a second distinctive word from the verse.

Why compare translations

Translations differ in how literally they follow the original wording and in how they phrase it for modern readers. Putting two or three side by side is one of the simplest ways to understand a verse better, because a word that seems odd in one may be clearer in another. It also helps when you are studying a specific topic and want to see how a key word is rendered. ScriptureSearch makes that comparison part of the same search, rather than a separate trip to another site.

Where the text comes from

The listing says the app is based on bible-api.com, a popular online Bible tool. That means ScriptureSearch fetches verses online, so expect to need an internet connection for searches.

Sharing what you find

Once you have the verse you were looking for, you can send it on directly: through social media, by email or as a text message. It is handy for sending a verse to a friend, a study group or a family chat without copying and pasting.

A simple way to use it

  1. Search a phrase you half remember, or type a reference.
  2. Open the verse you meant.
  3. Compare it in another translation.
  4. Share it with whoever needs it.

Good to know

  • Ads: the app contains ads.
  • In-app purchases: none are listed.
  • Connection: verses come from an online Bible tool, so searches need internet access.

  • You like comparing how different translations phrase the same passage.
  • You share verses with friends, family or a study group.
