item.title: remember vs rememberSaveable vs ViewModel: what survives what
item.description: Learn which state holder survives rotation, process death, or app closure in Jetpack Compose. Stop losing draft text and scroll positions with the right choice.
item.content:encoded:
Most developers assume that if they declare a variable inside a composable, it will persist as long as the screen is visible. That is the trap. You write var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }, expect the counter to hold its value when you rotate the phone or switch dark mode, and then watch it snap back to zero. The issue is not that Compose is broken; it is that you picked a holder that only survives recomposition, while your device performed a configuration change that recreated the entire Activity.

The book Compose Without the Confusion opens its state chapter with exactly this distinction under the heading "How long does state live?". This post covers the four main holders, what each one survives, and the exact commands or settings you need to use to match your data to the right container.

One caveat, straight from the book: this guidance applies to standard Android configuration changes and process death. Your specific app architecture may require additional layers, so check the sections on ViewModels and databases if your state needs to survive beyond the screen.

The trap: confusing recomposition with configuration changes

The usual way people find out their state is too fragile is that they rotate the phone and see their UI reset. The book explains that remember survives only recomposition. Recomposition happens when Compose needs to redraw a composable because its inputs changed, but the Activity itself remains alive. When you rotate the device, switch dark mode, or change the system language, Android recreates the Activity. This destroys the composition tree entirely.

If your state is held in remember, it vanishes with the old Activity. You might think adding mutableStateOf fixes it, but writing val count = mutableStateOf(0) without remember means the holder is recreated on every recomposition anyway, resetting the value immediately. You need both an observable holder and a mechanism to keep it across recreations.

The fix for temporary UI state is rememberSaveable. It is remember that also writes the value into the saved instance state. This allows it to survive configuration changes and process death for Bundle-able values like numbers, strings, booleans, and parcelable types.

var draftName by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
var showDeleteDialog by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }

A good rule of thumb from the book is to use remember or rememberSaveable for UI element state, such as whether a menu is expanded, the scroll position, or a draft in a text field. These values live in the composable and do not need to persist after the app closes.

The trap: expecting ViewModel to save everything

Many developers move all state into a ViewModel, assuming it will solve all persistence problems. This is partially correct but incomplete. A ViewModel survives configuration changes on its own, meaning your data stays intact when you rotate the phone. However, the book notes that a ViewModel does not survive process death on its own. If the system kills your app while it is in the background, the ViewModel is destroyed along with the Activity.

If your state comes from data or business rules, such as a list of items fetched from an API or whether a save operation succeeded, it belongs in a ViewModel. This keeps your UI composables stateless and testable. You hoist the state up to the lowest common ancestor of everything that reads or writes it.

// Stateless: easy to preview, test and reuse
@Composable
fun AddItemBar(
    name: String,
    onNameChange: (String) -> Unit,
    onAdd: () -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
) {
    Row(
        modifier = modifier.padding(16.dp),
        verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically,
    ) {
        OutlinedTextField(
            value = name,
            onValueChange = onNameChange,
            label = { Text("New item") },
            singleLine = true,
            modifier = Modifier.weight(1f),
        )
        Spacer(Modifier.width(8.dp))
        Button(onClick = onAdd, enabled = name.isNotBlank()) { Text("Add") }
    }
}

This pattern separates the UI from the state ownership. The parent owns the state and passes it down; the child sends events up. If the state needs to survive the app being closed, you must move it out of the ViewModel and into a persistent storage solution like Room or DataStore.

The trap: mutating objects instead of replacing them

Another common failure mode is assuming Compose will detect changes when you modify an object in place. Compose notices when a State holder gets a new value, but it does not notice when you reach into the old value and change it. Mutable objects that are not observable, such as an ArrayList or a mutable data class, do not trigger recomposition and show stale data.

// Wrong: mutates the list in place, Compose sees the same object
val items = remember { mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<PantryItem>()) }
items.value.add(newItem)                       // nothing recomposes

The fix is to treat UI state as values. You should replace the value with a new immutable list or use an observable list type provided by Compose. For data classes, you use copy() instead of setting fields directly.

// Right: replace the value with a new immutable list
var items by remember { mutableStateOf(listOf<PantryItem>()) }
items = items + newItem

// Also right: an observable list
val items = remember { mutableStateListOf<PantryItem>() }
items.add(newItem)

// Updating one item in a data class: copy, do not set fields
items = items.map { if (it.id == id) it.copy(quantity = it.quantity + 1) else it }

This ensures that every time the list content changes, Compose receives a new reference and triggers recomposition for the affected components.

Checklist

  • Use remember for state that only needs to survive recomposition within the same Activity instance.
  • Use rememberSaveable for UI element state like drafts or scroll positions that must survive rotation and process death.
  • Remember that rememberSaveable works out of the box for Bundle-able types; use a custom Saver for complex objects.
  • Hoist state to the lowest common ancestor that needs it, passing values down and events up via lambdas.
  • Use ViewModel for screen state derived from data or business rules that must survive configuration changes.
  • Know that ViewModel does not survive process death; use Room or DataStore for persistent storage.
  • Replace mutable lists with immutable lists or mutableStateListOf to trigger recomposition on change.
  • Never call suspend functions directly in the composable body; wrap them in LaunchedEffect with appropriate keys.

item.title: The trap of the version code reset
item.description: You set a version code in CI to prevent duplicates, but the workflow recreation resets the counter, forcing you to use a code Play has already rejected.
item.content:encoded:
Most developers set a version code in CI to guarantee that every upload is unique. That is the trap. A workflow recreation resets the counter to 1, so every new run tries to upload a version code Play has already seen, and the upload is refused. You might see the error message in the console or the Play Console, but you might not realize the root cause is the counter resetting. The book's example shows a workflow that computes the code using the CI run number, which starts at 1. This number would create a conflict with the manual release, and Play rejects any code at or below the live one.

The book "Pass Google Play Review" explains that versionCode must be a positive integer, each release must use a greater value than the one before, and Play refuses an upload that reuses a code. The greatest value Google Play allows is 2100000000. If you compute the code from the CI run number, you discover the app's first release was uploaded by hand with a higher code, so every automated upload is refused. The trap is that you think you are being safe by enforcing uniqueness, but you are actually creating a conflict with the manual release. You must ensure your code always increases and stays far below the limit.

The rule: pass the code in from the build

The book recommends the safest pattern for automated releases: pass the version code in from the build, with a fallback for local builds. You do not hardcode the number in the source. This approach ensures the build system pulls the number from the environment. If the environment variable is missing, it falls back to 1 for local development. This separation of concerns keeps your build configuration clean and allows you to control the version number in your CI pipeline.

android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = System.getenv("VERSION_CODE")?.toIntOrNull() ?: 1
        versionName = System.getenv("VERSION_NAME") ?: "0.1.0"
    }
}

This configuration reads the version code from the environment variable VERSION_CODE. If the variable is not present, it defaults to 1. This is useful for local builds where you might not have the CI environment variables set. However, for CI builds, you must provide the variable. This pattern prevents you from hardcoding a specific number that might conflict with existing releases.

The trap: the CI run number resets

The book warns that a CI run number restarts when the workflow is recreated. If you compute the code from the clock in CI, you rely on a counter that can start over. The book shows an example of this pitfall in the "CaptionBurn" workflow. The workflow in chartmann1590/captionburn computes the code exactly this way. The workflow's own run counter starts at 1 and would undercut the version code already live on Play (116, published manually). Play rejects any code at or below the live one.

CODE=$(date -u +'%y%j%H%M')
echo "VERSION_CODE=$CODE" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

The comment in the workflow explains why: the workflow's own run counter starts at 1 and would undercut the version code already live on Play. Its first successful automated release used version code 262850104 and versionName 0.1.20261012.0104. The trap is that the workflow counter is not persistent. When you recreate the workflow, the counter goes back to 1. If you are already past 116, the new code will be rejected. You need a number that is guaranteed to be unique and larger than the previous one.

The fix: compute from the clock, not the counter

The book suggests computing the code from the clock in CI so it only ever goes up. You should use a date-based code that always increases and stays far below the limit. The example in the book uses the year, day of year, and time in UTC. This method guarantees that every new build gets a unique, increasing number. It does not rely on a workflow counter that can restart. The Dosely workflow takes the opposite approach and asks for the code as a manual input, with a description that tells you to check App bundle explorer for the highest code already used.

# yy + day of year + HHMM in UTC, e.g. 262850104 (2026, day 285, 01:04)
CODE=$(date -u +'%y%j%H%M')
echo "VERSION_CODE=$CODE" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

This code calculates the version code based on the current UTC date and time. The format is yy (year), j (day of year), H (hour), M (minute). This ensures that every build gets a unique number based on when it was built. Since the date and time always increase, the version code will never decrease or repeat. This is the safest way to generate version codes in CI, as described in the book.

item.title: Lock the Firewall Admin Page
item.description: A fresh OPNsense install is wide open. This guide moves the web interface to HTTPS and the management network only.
item.content:encoded:
A fresh OPNsense install is built to be reachable so you can set it up: the web interface listens on every interface, an anti-lockout rule keeps the LAN side open to it no matter what you configure, and you log in as root with a password. Most people never revisit any of that. The result is a firewall whose own admin page is one of the most exposed services in the house.

The book opens its hardening chapter with this exact scenario. Every zone you create gives the firewall another address, and by default its web interface and any other service it runs answer on all of them. A smart plug on the IoT network should not be able to load the login page of the device that decides what it is allowed to do.

The trap: the default open door

The trap is that the default configuration assumes you are in the same room as the firewall. It assumes you are on the LAN, and it assumes you will remember to lock the door later. The book points out that until you create VLANs (Chapter 3), the existing LAN interface plays the role of the management network. This means the firewall listens on the LAN interface by default, and the anti-lockout rule allows access from anywhere on the LAN.

This setup is convenient for setup, but it is a security risk. The anti-lockout rule is designed to prevent you from locking yourself out of the firewall by mistake, but it is a blanket permission. It allows the web interface from anywhere on the LAN, which means any device on your LAN can attempt to log in. The book warns that a fresh install is built to be reachable, and the result is a firewall whose own admin page is one of the most exposed services in the house.

The fix: move the web interface

The solution is to move the web interface to a dedicated management network and force HTTPS. The book recommends creating an alias for the machines that may administer the network, so every rule can refer to it by name. This makes it easier to manage who has access to the firewall.

Create an alias for the machines that may administer the network, so every rule can refer to it by name. Firewall, then Aliases, add:

Name: ADMIN_HOSTS Type: Host(s) Content: 192.168.10.21 192.168.10.22 Description: Machines allowed to manage network gear

Give those machines fixed DHCP reservations so their addresses never change underneath the alias.

Next, move the web interface. System, then Settings, then Administration. The settings that matter:

• Protocol: HTTPS, with a certificate you trust. The self-signed one works; a certificate from your own CA (System, then Trust) or from the ACME plugin for a hostname like fw.example.com removes the browser warning, which matters because people who click through warnings stop noticing the one that is real. • HTTP Strict Transport Security: on, once HTTPS is working. • Listen interfaces: choose the management interface only (and the LAN while you migrate). The default, all interfaces, is what you are fixing. • Session timeout: a short value such as 30 minutes, so an unattended browser tab does not stay logged in.

Then add an explicit rule that lets your admin machines in, before you remove the anti-lockout rule. On the management interface (or LAN for now), Firewall, then Rules:

Action: Pass Source: ADMIN_HOSTS Destination: This Firewall Port: HTTPS (443), and SSH (22) if you use it Description: Admin access to firewall

Test it from an admin machine. Only then tick Disable anti-lockout on the Administration page. The anti-lockout rule allows the web interface from anywhere on the LAN; with your own rule in place, it has done its job.

The fix: two-factor login

A password alone is one phishing page away from gone. OPNsense has time-based one-time passwords (TOTP) built in, the same six-digit codes as any authenticator app. The book recommends enabling this for any admin user.

  1. System, then Access, then Servers: add a server of type Local + Timebased One Time Password. The defaults (6 digits, 30 seconds) suit standard authenticator apps.
  2. System, then Access, then Users: edit your admin user, tick to generate an OTP seed, save, and scan the QR code it shows with your authenticator app.
  1. Open the web interface in a private browser window and test the login before you change anything else. With the default token order, you type the six-digit code followed by your password in the password field, with no space; the server's "reverse token order" option flips that.
  2. System, then Settings, then Administration: set the authentication server to the new TOTP server.

Keep a second way in. Save the OTP seed in your password manager, and remember that the console login is separate and does not use the web interface's authentication server.

The fix: named admin and SSH

Create your own user in the admins group and use it day to day, so the logs show who changed what. Keep the root account with a long random password stored in your password manager, and use it only at the console.

If you do not use SSH on the firewall, leave it off; it is off by default. If you do, System, then Settings, then Administration, Secure Shell section:

• Root login: off. Log in as your named admin user. • Password login: off. Paste your public key into your user's Authorized keys field first, and test a key login in a second terminal before you turn passwords off. • Listen interfaces: management only.

The fix: close unused doors

The book also advises closing what you are not using. This includes the console menu, UPnP, and the WAN interface.

• Console menu password. On the Administration page, protect the console menu with a password. Anyone with physical or hypervisor access to the console otherwise gets a root menu. • UPnP. OPNsense does not ship UPnP enabled; it is a plugin (os-upnp). Leave it uninstalled unless a game console truly needs it, and if it does, limit it to that one device's address with the plugin's access rules. • WAN. Check that the WAN interface keeps Block private networks and Block bogon networks ticked (the defaults), that no rule on WAN passes traffic to "This Firewall" except the WireGuard port you will add in Chapter 6, and that nothing in the services list listens on WAN. • Unused services. Look through Services and turn off anything you set up to try once.

Checklist: the front door

☐ ADMIN_HOSTS alias created, with DHCP reservations for those machines ☐ Web interface on HTTPS, listening on management (and LAN while migrating) ☐ Explicit admin rule tested, then the anti-lockout rule disabled ☐ TOTP login tested in a private window, seed saved in the password manager ☐ Named admin user in use; root for the console only; SSH off or key-only ☐ Console menu password set; UPnP not installed (or limited to one device) ☐ WAN blocks private and bogon networks; nothing administrative on WAN

item.title: Database inside a VM? Dump it before the backup
item.description: Your VM backup has a database inside. The trap is trusting the VM backup alone for an application with a database.
item.content:encoded:
Your VM backup has a database inside. The trap is trusting the VM backup alone for an application with a database. The backup captures the state of the VM's disk at a moment in time. With the guest agent installed, snapshot mode flushes the filesystem, which is usually enough. Usually is not a word the book likes in a backup chapter.

The book covers this under the heading "Backing Up the Things Proxmox Can't See." A whole-VM backup of Home Assistant is a perfect copy of the VM. It is also 32 GB to move around when all you wanted was yesterday's automations, and it does not help when you want to move Home Assistant to a different machine entirely. The same goes for OPNsense: the VM is replaceable, the config is not. And inside your Docker guests there are databases that do not like being copied mid-write. Each of these wants its own, smaller, application-level backup on top of the VM backup.

The trap: trusting the snapshot

The trap is the belief that a Proxmox snapshot captures a consistent state. The book notes that the guest agent installed on the VM flushes the filesystem, which is usually enough. Usually is not enough when a database is mid-write. A transaction can be half-applied to the log files, leading to corruption on restore. The fix is to run a database dump a few minutes before the Proxmox backup so the VM backup contains a consistent copy even if the live files were mid-write.

The fix: dump the database before the backup

For any guest running Postgres, MariaDB or SQLite under Docker, add a dump to the inventory. The dump runs a few minutes before the Proxmox backup, lands on the guest's disk, and gets picked up by the backup like any other file. The VM backup then contains a consistent dump even if the live database files were mid-write.

Immich's own documentation gives the exact command, and it is the one the book recommends:

docker exec -t immich_postgres \ pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists --username=postgres \ | zstd > /srv/backup/immich-db-$(date +%F).sql.zst

find /srv/backup -name 'immich-db-*' -mtime +14 -delete

For Vaultwarden, stop the container or use SQLite's own .backup command against the live file; a plain cp of a busy SQLite database can land between pages. For Nextcloud, turn on maintenance mode, dump the database, turn it off. All three are a few lines in a script on a systemd timer at 02:00, half an hour ahead of the 02:30 backup job.

The fix: backup the firewall config separately

OPNsense keeps its entire state in one file, /conf/config.xml, and it offers to back that file up for you. System, then Configuration, then Backups. Download gives you the file now. Tick Encrypt this configuration file and set a password; the file contains every secret the firewall knows, including VPN keys and the admin password hash.

Google Drive and Nextcloud backup are built in on that same page: the firewall uploads the config whenever it changes. Nextcloud is the better fit if you self-host it (the book covers the setup); a dedicated Nextcloud user with one shared folder is enough. The os-git-backup plugin pushes every configuration change as a commit to a Git repository you host. Every change becomes a diff you can read, which is worth more than it sounds when a rule you do not remember writing starts blocking something.

You also keep OPNsense in the weekly vzdump job. A restore from the VM backup is the quickest way back if the VM breaks. A restore from config.xml onto a fresh install is the way back if the hardware changes: install OPNsense, assign the interfaces, then System, then Configuration, then Backups, then Restore. The one thing to know in advance is interface names. A new VM with different NIC order will not match vtnet0 and vtnet1 in the file, and you will reassign interfaces at the console before the GUI comes back.

The fix: back up the host config

The nodes are the one thing nothing above protects. /etc/pve holds every guest config, the storage definitions, the backup jobs, user accounts and the cluster configuration; /etc/network/interfaces holds the bridges and VLANs that took an afternoon to get right. Chapter 3 shows the proxmox-backup-client command that sends both to PBS nightly. If you are not running PBS, a tarball to the NAS does the job:

tar czf /mnt/pve/nas-backup/host-$(hostname)-$(date +%F).tgz \ /etc/pve /etc/network/interfaces /etc/hosts /etc/vzdump.conf /etc/apt

Add the output of pvesm status, zpool status and lsblk -f to a text file next to it. On a rebuild, those three listings answer every "what was that storage called?" question.

Checklist: beyond Proxmox

☐ Home Assistant automatic daily backups on, encrypted, emergency kit saved ☐ HA backups going to at least one location other than its own disk (NAS or B2) ☐ OPNsense config.xml backed up on change to Nextcloud, Google Drive or Git, plus an encrypted download after big changes ☐ A database dump before the backup window for every guest with a database ☐ The nodes' /etc/pve and network config backed up nightly ☐ A text file of storage, pool and disk layouts kept with the host backup

item.title: Don't keep secrets in Auto Backup
item.description: The backup rules file excludes device-bound files, but you must also set android:allowBackup="false" to prevent cloud backups from moving ciphertext.
item.content:encoded:
Most developers assume that because they are using a secure key generation system, their app is safe. They write the code to pull a key from the Android Keystore, encrypt a token, and store the result in a private file. They then look at the Android documentation for Auto Backup and see that it only copies files from filesDir and getExternalFilesDir(). They conclude that the ciphertext is safe because it sits in a private directory. This is the trap. The platform treats the private directory as a black box, but Auto Backup ignores that rule and sweeps the ciphertext into the Google Drive backup as soon as the key is generated inside the Android Keystore.

The "Data That Survives" chapter opens its backup section with exactly this distinction, under a heading that sums it up: two kinds of transfer, two sections in one rules file. This post covers the data extraction rules, what the cloud backup actually includes, and the setting that stops it from moving ciphertext.

The trap: ciphertext travels in the cloud

The Android Auto Backup feature copies most of your app's private files to the user's Google Drive, protected by their Google Account credentials. According to the guide, the backup is end-to-end encrypted on Android 9 and higher using the device's PIN, pattern or password. The default behavior includes shared preferences, files in filesDir, databases and files in getExternalFilesDir(). It excludes the cache directories and getNoBackupFilesDir().

For an offline-first app that is mostly good news: unsynced notes can survive a lost phone. It also means your database restores onto a new device, which affects sync state, and that anything secret or device-bound travels too unless you exclude it.

The trap is that the Android Keystore key material never leaves secure hardware where available, but the ciphertext it produces does. A Keystore key does not travel in backups or device transfers, so ciphertext restored onto a new phone cannot be decrypted there. If you rely on Auto Backup to move the ciphertext, you are effectively sending the secret to the cloud without the key.

The fix: disable Auto Backup for the app

The chapter provides a single, direct setting to close this gap. The guide warns that for apps targeting Android 12 or higher, on some manufacturers' devices that disables cloud backup but not device-to-device transfer, so the rules file is the more precise tool. The first step is to set the manifest attribute to false.

The guide advises setting this attribute in the `` tag.

The fix: exclude device-bound files from the rules

Even with android:allowBackup="false", you should configure the data extraction rules file. This file controls what goes to Google Drive and what happens during a direct phone-to-phone move. For apps targeting Android 12 (API 31) and higher, the rules live in a data extraction rules file referenced from the manifest. The guide also tells you to keep a second, older-format file (android:fullBackupContent) for devices running Android 11 and lower.

The manifest entry for the application tag references these files.

<application
    android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules"
    android:fullBackupContent="@xml/backup_rules_legacy">

You then define the rules in the XML file. The chapter presents a complete example that includes the cloud backup section and the device-transfer section. The example lists the database and settings file to include, but explicitly excludes the secrets file.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<data-extraction-rules>
    <cloud-backup disableIfNoEncryptionCapabilities="true">
        <include domain="database" path="field-notes.db" />
        <include domain="file" path="datastore/settings.json" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="datastore/secrets.pb" />
    </cloud-backup>
    <device-transfer>
        <include domain="database" path="field-notes.db" />
        <include domain="file" path="datastore/settings.json" />
        <exclude domain="file" path="datastore/secrets.pb" />
    </device-transfer>
</data-extraction-rules>

The exclude tag for the secrets file is the precise command that enforces the rule. It tells the system to keep the ciphertext out of both the cloud backup and the device transfer. The disableIfNoEncryptionCapabilities="true" attribute on the cloud-backup tag skips the backup when it cannot be end-to-end encrypted, adding another layer of protection.

Checklist

  • Set android:allowBackup="false" in the manifest to disable Auto Backup.
  • Create a data extraction rules file referenced from the manifest.
  • Use `` to stop ciphertext from traveling.
  • List every file that should travel using `` tags.
  • Remember that a database restored from backup carries its dirty flags and server_version numbers, so test the restore onto a fresh install.

item.description: WarmWord is an Android AI companion and journal that runs its model on your device, works in your language and surfaces crisis resources fast.
item.content:encoded:
Some thoughts are easier to say out loud than to keep circling. When anxious, racing or lonely thoughts get heavy, having somewhere to put them helps, even if it is not a person. WarmWord is an AI companion and journal for those moments, built so the conversation stays on your phone.

First, the important part, in the app's own spirit: WarmWord is not a substitute for professional care. In an emergency, contact your local emergency services.

What it does

  • A companion that listens without judgment. Chat whenever your thoughts feel too heavy to carry alone.
  • On-device AI. The model runs entirely on your device, so your conversations stay yours.
  • Your language, all the way through. Menus, buttons, screens and WarmWord's replies, translated by a small on-device model.
  • Journaling. A calm space to reflect and untangle the day.
  • Mood insights. Gentle insights that show patterns over time.
  • Crisis resources. Helpline and crisis resources surfaced in seconds when you need them.
  • Personal touches. Choose tones and set reminders.

Why on-device matters here

What you say to a mental health companion is about as personal as data gets. WarmWord's answer is to keep the AI on your phone. The chat model runs locally, and the translation model that puts the app into your language runs locally too, so, according to the listing, nothing leaves your device for either. If you have avoided apps like this because of where your words might end up, that design is the main reason to look at this one.

Using it in your own language

Pick a language during onboarding or later in settings. A small translation model on the phone then translates the whole app, including the companion's replies, not just the menus. You get the same experience in your language without an online translation service in the loop.

Chat, journal, notice

The pieces work best together:

  1. Chat when something is weighing on you right now and you want a response.
  2. Journal when you want to slow down and write the day out for yourself.
  3. Check your mood insights now and then to spot quiet patterns, like which days tend to be harder.

Reminders can nudge you to check in, and you can adjust the tone of the companion so it feels right to you.

When you need more than an app

WarmWord keeps crisis and helpline resources a few seconds away. If you are in danger or someone else is, use them, or call your local emergency services. A companion app can be a place to think. It cannot replace a professional, and it is not meant to.

item.title: Reach your homelab from anywhere safely
item.description: Stop forwarding ports to everything. Use Tailscale for secure remote access.
item.content:encoded:
Port forwarding your homelab to the internet is how you end up in someone's botnet. A mesh VPN fixes remote access properly: every device gets a private address, connections are encrypted end to end, and nothing listens on your public IP. Tailscale is the easiest way there, and its free tier covers a homelab comfortably. The trap is opening ports to every service you run. You might think this makes things easier, but it creates a massive surface for attacks. When you forward ports, you are inviting strangers to test your firewalls. You do not need to expose every admin interface to the open internet. A mesh VPN keeps everything inside a private tunnel. The book explains that you should never forward ports for admin interfaces, because a compromised port gives an attacker direct access to the machine.

Where to install it

You have three options, and the best answer is usually a mix:

• On each machine you want to reach: your laptop, phone, the Proxmox hosts and a few key VMs. Simple and precise. • A subnet router: one node that advertises your whole LAN, so devices that can't run Tailscale (printers, cameras, IoT gear) become reachable. • On the firewall: OPNsense has a Tailscale plugin, which works, but it ties remote access to the firewall's health. A small dedicated container is often more resilient.

The trap here is putting everything on one machine. If that node goes down, you lose access to your whole network. You might see this when your laptop cannot ping a printer or a camera because the Tailscale node is offline. The fix is to distribute the load. Run Tailscale on multiple machines. The book advises running it on the Proxmox hosts and a subnet router container. This ensures that if one node fails, another can take over.

A subnet router in an LXC container

Unprivileged containers need access to the TUN device. On the Proxmox host, add to /etc/pve/lxc/.conf:

lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow: c 10:200 rwm lxc.mount.entry: /dev/net/tun dev/net/tun none bind,create=file

Then inside the container:

curl -fsSL | sh echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' > /etc/sysctl.d/99-tailscale.conf echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1' >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-tailscale.conf sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-tailscale.conf

tailscale up --advertise-routes=192.168.10.0/24,10.30.0.0/24 --ssh

The trap is assuming the container can connect automatically. You might run the commands and find that the container cannot reach the TUN device, or that the routes do not actually make your LAN devices reachable. You see this when you try to ping an IP address from your laptop and get a timeout, even though the container is running. The fix involves granting the container access to the device and enabling forwarding. The book provides the exact commands to enable IP forwarding and set up the routes. You must approve the routes in the Tailscale admin console ( Machines → … → Edit route settings). On Linux clients that should use them, run tailscale up --accept-routes. Phones and laptops accept them by default.

TIP No TUN device available? tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking runs Tailscale entirely in user space. It's slower, but it works in restrictive containers, and it can expose a SOCKS5 proxy for tools that need to reach your tailnet.

Settings worth changing on day one

• Disable key expiry on servers and subnet routers (admin console → machine → Disable key expiry). Otherwise they drop off the tailnet every 180 days, usually while you're traveling. • Use MagicDNS, so you reach machines by name instead of memorizing 100.x addresses. • Write an access policy. The default lets every device reach every other device. Tighten it with tags, so your phone can reach Home Assistant but a shared laptop can't reach your Proxmox UI. • Turn on Tailscale SSH (--ssh) for servers, and stop exposing SSH anywhere else. • Pick an exit node for public Wi-Fi: any Linux node with --advertise-exit-node can route your laptop's traffic through your home connection.

The trap is using the default settings. The default policy allows every device to reach every other device. This is dangerous if you share a laptop with others. You might see that your phone can suddenly access Proxmox, even though you did not intend to give it that permission. The book advises writing an access policy with tags. You can tighten it so your phone can reach Home Assistant but a shared laptop cannot reach your Proxmox UI. Another trap is leaving key expiry enabled. You might find that your servers drop off the tailnet after 180 days. The fix is to disable key expiry on servers and subnet routers. This keeps them connected permanently. You should also turn on Tailscale SSH for servers and stop exposing SSH anywhere else.

Don't make it a single point of failure

If Tailscale is your only way in, have a second path. Run Tailscale on two machines that advertise the same routes (Tailscale will fail over between subnet routers), and keep it on the Proxmox host itself, so you can still reach the console when every VM is down.

The trap is relying solely on one node. If that single node crashes or loses internet, you lose access to your homelab entirely. You might see this when you lose connection while traveling and cannot reach any of your services. The book warns that if Tailscale is your only way in, you have a single point of failure. The fix is to have a second path. Run Tailscale on two machines that advertise the same routes. Tailscale will fail over between subnet routers. You should also keep it on the Proxmox host itself, so you can still reach the console when every VM is down.

Checklist: remote access

☐ No inbound port forwards for admin interfaces ☐ Tailscale on the Proxmox hosts plus a subnet router container ☐ Routes approved; key expiry disabled on servers ☐ Access policy with tags, not the allow-all default ☐ A second way in that doesn't depend on any single VM
